comparison: Both strongly support the selective increase in Ly6Clo monocytes (C3, C43, C48, C49) with no changes in Ly6Chi monocytes or neutrophils. OpenEval additionally evaluates C53 and C58, while peer review includes C119. Both reference Figure 1A flow cytometry data as primary evidence.

Both support the finding that BM and spleen monocyte populations are unchanged (C50, C51, C55). OpenEval additionally evaluates C56 (inference about BM origin) and C57 (BM egress rates), which peer reviewers accept implicitly without detailed discussion.

Both support the negative findings that RBP-J does not affect monocyte survival, proliferation, or conversion (C59, C61, C62, C63, C64, C67, C68). OpenEval does not evaluate conversion claims C72-C73 in this result, while peer review groups all negative mechanistic findings together. Both praise the use of multiple complementary assays.

Both support the adoptive transfer data showing no difference in Ly6Chi to Ly6Clo conversion (C71, C72, C73). OpenEval notes limitations (single timepoint, specific recipient model), while peer reviewers accept this as part of the broader negative mechanistic findings without specific concerns.

Both strongly support the cell-intrinsic nature of RBP-J regulation (C5, C42, C76, C77, C83, C121) using BMT and parabiosis data. OpenEval additionally evaluates C75, C78, while peer review includes C81. All reviewers praise the use of technically challenging methods as a major strength.

Both support the finding of increased CCR2 expression in RBP-J-deficient monocytes (C4, C84, C85, C88, C90, C122) based on RNA-seq and validation experiments. OpenEval additionally evaluates C86 and C89. Both note the data is well-supported, though OpenEval explicitly mentions the direct vs. indirect mechanism is not established.

Major disagreement on CCR2 genetic rescue interpretation (C9, C92, C93, C94, C95, C98, C123). OpenEval finds claims strongly supported and considers CCR2 a key downstream mediator. Peer reviewers express significant concerns, noting the experiment lacks important controls, CCR2 deletion doesn't remove the Ly6Clo bias, and the mechanistic link remains correlative. Peer review rates this as UNCERTAIN vs. OpenEval's SUPPORTED.
Both support the finding that CD11c downregulation persists in DKO mice (C96, C97), indicating CCR2-independent regulation. Complete agreement with no concerns raised by either evaluation.

Both support the finding of increased Ly6Clo monocytes and CD16.2+ IM in lungs (C7, C8, C44, C45, C103, C104, C120). OpenEval additionally evaluates C105. Both reference Figure 6 data without challenge and accept the selective nature of the increases.

Both support the negative finding that lung monocyte proliferation is unchanged (C106, C107). Both evaluations accept this as evidence against local proliferation and in support of the recruitment hypothesis. Complete agreement.

Both support the LPS challenge data showing enhanced recruitment (C111, C112). OpenEval additionally evaluates C109. Both accept the experimental design and results without challenge, demonstrating functional consequences of the phenotype.

Disagreement on lung CCR2 rescue interpretation (C113, C114, C115, C116, C117, C118). OpenEval finds strong support for CCR2-dependent recruitment. Peer reviewers express concerns that CCR2 ablation only has partial effects, the Ly6Clo bias may persist in DKO, and statements about cell origin may lack compelling evidence. Peer review rates as UNCERTAIN vs. OpenEval's SUPPORTED.

OpenEval evaluates the main conclusions of the study (C10, C46, C154) as well-supported by convergence of multiple experimental approaches. No corresponding peer review result specifically addresses these overarching conclusion claims, though peer reviewers generally support the main findings with caveats about CCR2 mechanism.

Peer reviewers raise concerns about RBP-J knockout efficiency (C47), noting qPCR shows only two-thirds knockdown when complete loss is expected. This technical concern affects confidence in attributing phenotypes to RBP-J loss. OpenEval does not evaluate this claim.

Peer reviewers support the parabiosis finding showing competitive advantage of RBP-J-deficient cells (C6, C152). OpenEval does not have a separate result for these specific claims, though related cell-intrinsic claims are evaluated in R5.
